Read this scene from a novel and say what it tells us about time. Don't work out a day number: only what the text says.

## End of the Previous Scene

Quite satisfied, he closed his door, and locked himself in; double-locked himself in, which was not his custom. Thus secured against surprise, he took off his cravat; put on his dressing-gown and slippers, and his nightcap; and sat down before the fire to take his gruel. It was a very low fire indeed; nothing on such a bitter night. He was obliged to sit close to it, and brood over it, before he could extract the least sensation of warmth from such a handful of fuel. The fireplace was an old one, built by some Dutch merchant long ago, and paved all round with quaint Dutch tiles, designed to illustrate the Scriptures. There were Cains and Abels, Pharaoh's daughters; Queens of Sheba, Angelic messengers descending through the air on clouds like feather-beds, Abrahams, Belshazzars, Apostles putting off to sea in butter-boats, hundreds of figures to attract his thoughts; and yet that face of Marley, seven years dead, came like the ancient Prophet's rod, and swallowed up the whole. If each smooth tile had been a blank at first, with power to shape some picture on its surface from the disjointed fragments of his thoughts, there would have been a copy of old Marley's head on every one. "Humbug!" said Scrooge; and walked across the room.

## Scene: marley-ghost-arrives

After several turns, he sat down again. As he threw his head back in the chair, his glance happened to rest upon a bell, a disused bell, that hung in the room, and communicated for some purpose now forgotten with a chamber in the highest story of the building. It was with great astonishment, and with a strange, inexplicable dread, that as he looked, he saw this bell begin to swing. It swung so softly in the outset that it scarcely made a sound; but soon it rang out loudly, and so did every bell in the house.

This might have lasted half a minute, or a minute, but it seemed an hour. The bells ceased as they had begun, together. They were succeeded by a clanking noise, deep down below; as if some person were dragging a heavy chain over the casks in the wine-merchant's cellar. Scrooge then remembered to have heard that ghosts in haunted houses were described as dragging chains.

The garret-door flew open with a booming sound, and then he heard the noise much louder, on the floors above; then coming down the stairs; then coming straight towards his door.

"It's humbug still!" said Scrooge. "I won't believe it."

His colour changed though, when, without a pause, it came on through the heavy door, and passed into the room before his eyes. Upon its coming in, the dying flame leaped up, as though it cried, "I know him; Marley's Ghost!" and fell again.

The same face: the very same. Marley in his pigtail, usual waistcoat, tights and boots; the tassels on the latter bristling, like his pigtail, and his coat-skirts, and the hair upon his head. The chain he drew was clasped about his middle. It was long, and wound about him like a tail; and it was made (for Scrooge observed it closely) of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel. His body was transparent; so that Scrooge, observing him, and looking through his waistcoat, could see the two buttons on his coat behind.

Scrooge had often heard it said that Marley had no bowels, but he had never believed it until now.

No, nor did he believe it even now. Though he looked the phantom through and through, and saw it standing before him; though he felt the chilling influence of its death-cold eyes; and marked the very texture of the folded kerchief bound about its head and chin, which wrapper he had not observed before; he was still incredulous, and fought against his senses.



## Instructions

Output each field on its own labeled line.

TIME_RELATION: [when this scene happens relative to the scene before it in reading order — one of: continues (picks up at the same time or moments later), later (some time after it), earlier (before it: a flashback or a recollection told as a scene, including a past that a spirit, dream or vision shows a character; also a scene whose present is only a line or a short lead-in before it mostly tells the past, such as a story a character tells or the narrator's account of someone's youth, but not one where the present has real action on the page around the telling), frame (narration from after the story, looking back), vision (events that have not happened, or may not happen, as the story tells them: a prophecy, a future a character is shown that may be averted, a dream of what might come; the past is always earlier, even when a spirit, a dream or a vision shows it), unclear]
TIME_GAP: [the gap from the previous scene in at most six words, no explanation: "an hour", "the next morning", "three weeks", "five years", "several weeks"; empty if none is stated or implied]
TIME_ANCHOR: [a calendar fact pinning when THIS scene's action happens — a date, weekday, month, season, holiday or named day ("the hottest day of the summer") — quoted briefly; not a habit ("every Friday") or a date the scene only mentions; empty if none]
TIME_REFERS: [any statement in this scene of how long ago or how long until another event in the story, quoted briefly: "that June night three months before", "five years since he'd seen her", "the funeral was on the third day"; separate several with semicolons; empty if none]
TIME_SPAN: [when the scene summarizes a stretch of time ("all that summer"), how long; empty for a scene that plays out in one sitting]
TIME_DATE: [only what this scene's own text states about the calendar date, in EDTF: "1922-07-04", "XXXX-07-04" when the year isn't given here, "1922" for a year, "1922-22" for summer 1922 (21 spring, 22 summer, 23 autumn, 24 winter), "1917~" for "around 1917", "1922-06/1922-09" for a stretch. A date the text fixes by a stated distance from a named calendar day counts as given, marked ~: "In two weeks it'll be the longest day in the year" → "XXXX-06-07~". Never fill in a part the text doesn't give; empty if the text gives no date]
